analysis.one_liner: Extends copyright terms by 20 years, keeping books, films, and songs locked up longer before they become free for public use.
analysis.headline: The House passed the copyright extension by voice vote on March 25, 1998; the Senate never voted on it, but the same 20-year extension became law that year through the Senate's companion bill.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill adds 20 years to every copyright: works by individual authors go from life plus 50 years to life plus 70 years, and corporate works go from 75 to 95 years. It applies to copyrights that already exist, so nothing new gets created in exchange — existing owners simply collect 20 more years of revenue, and the public waits 20 more years before works enter the public domain. It also carries a separate title making it easier for small businesses like restaurants and bars to play music without paying performing-rights societies.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of existing copyrights — film studios, music publishers, record labels, and authors' estates — gain 20 more years of exclusive revenue on works already created. A narrow library exemption and a music-licensing exemption for small businesses soften the blow slightly.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Film studios, music publishers, copyright estates

how_it_helps.text: Extends copyright for works created after 1977 from the author's life plus 50 years to life plus 70 years, and for corporate 'works for hire' from 75 years after publication to 95 years [S2][S5].
Applies retroactively: copyrights already in their renewal term get 95 years from the original grant, and works published before 2003 are protected through 2047 [S2][S5].
Lets authors or their heirs terminate old publishing licenses during the extended term and reclaim their rights [S2][S5].

Exempts restaurants, bars, and shops under 3,500 square feet from paying music-licensing fees to performing rights societies like ASCAP and BMI, and gives businesses a right to binding arbitration over disputed fees [S4][S5].

Allows libraries and archives to copy works during the final 20 years of their copyright term for preservation or scholarship, but only if the work is not commercially exploited or available at a reasonable price [S3][S5].
Requires anyone acquiring rights to a film made under union contracts to honor the residual payment obligations owed to writers, directors, and performers [S4][S5].

analysis.who_pays: Everyone who reads, watches, listens, teaches, or builds on older works: librarians, archivists, educators, documentary filmmakers, and future creators must wait 20 more years before works become free to use. Songwriters lose some royalty income from the small-business music exemption.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public — readers, libraries, teachers, future creators

drawbacks.text: Extending terms on works that already exist provides no incentive to create anything new; the only effect on the 99% of the value is 20 more years of private control over old works [S2].
The bill delays the public domain — the pool of works anyone may freely copy, quote, adapt, or republish — by two decades, which raises costs for educators, archivists, and independent creators.

The library exception is narrow: it only covers works with no commercial exploitation and copies unavailable at a reasonable price, and it does not extend to the public beyond the library itself [S3][S5].
The small-business music exemption shrinks royalty income for the songwriters whose works are performed [S4][S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall almost entirely on the public and fall immediately; the gains go almost entirely to owners of already-existing copyrights, with no new works produced in exchange. The small offsets — the library preservation exception, the small-business music exemption, and termination rights for authors' heirs — are real but minor next to a 20-year lock on the public domain.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by voice vote with no recorded opposition, but the Senate Judiciary Committee never voted on it; the Senate instead passed its own companion bill with the same extension, and that version was signed into law in October 1998.

narrative.text: The House Judiciary Committee reported the bill on March 18, 1998, and the House passed it by voice vote on March 25, 1998 [S4][S7].
The Senate received the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee, where it received no further action; the record points to the Senate's companion bill S.505 for further action [S7].

The substance — the 20-year extension — became law anyway when the Senate passed its companion version in October 1998 (widely reported; the Sonny Bono Copyright Term Extension Act, Public Law 105-298).
The House adopted the name 'Sonny Bono Copyright Term Extension Act' by unanimous consent after the bill passed [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major copyright holders came out ahead: entertainment companies, music publishers, and record labels collected 20 more years of exclusive revenue on existing catalogs, while the public waited two more decades for works to enter the public domain.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Film studios, music publishers, copyright owners

for.name: Rep. Howard Coble
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it through the House Judiciary Committee to passage.

for.name: House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Marked up and reported the bill by voice vote on March 18, 1998.

for.name: House Rules Committee and House leadership
for.what_they_did: Reported the rule that brought the bill to the floor under a structured process, allowing it to pass by voice vote the next day.

for.name: 12 cosponsors (6 Democrats, 6 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, split evenly between the parties.

for.name: Large entertainment and copyright industries
for.role: Film studios, music publishers, record labels
for.what_they_did: Lobbied heavily for the 20-year extension of existing copyright terms; the bill is widely known as the 'Mickey Mouse Protection Act' because it extended the protection of early Disney films and similar works.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the House bill and never reported it or brought it to a vote; the Senate advanced its own companion version instead.

against.name: Copyright scholars, libraries, and public-domain advocates
against.what_they_did: Argued that extending already-existing copyrights gives nothing to the public and locks up culture for two more decades; later challenged the law in court (Eldred v. Ashcroft) and lost.

sides.party_line_note: The House passed the bill by voice vote with no recorded division, and its 12 cosponsors split evenly, 6 Democrats and 6 Republicans [S6][S7].

industries.industry: Film studios and other large copyright holders
industries.note: A 20-year extension on existing works — including corporate works kept 95 years from publication — is a pure revenue windfall on catalogs already created. The public pays by waiting 20 more years for free access.
Sound recordings fixed before 1972 keep state-law protection until 2067, and musical compositions gain 20 years. Partly offset by the small-business exemption that shrinks performance royalties.
Title II exempts small establishments from paying performing-rights societies for background music and gives them binding arbitration over disputed fees.
The bill narrows what they can charge small businesses and adds mandatory arbitration. Their royalties support songwriters, so the loss partly reaches individual creators.
Extended terms and new termination rights let authors' families recapture rights from publishers, but most copyrighted works are owned by corporations, not individual authors.
They gain a narrow copying right for works in the final 20 years of protection, but lose far more from the two-decade delay of the public domain.
